To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the default time of a firm is a stopping time in the filtration generated by a price process that is correlated to the state variable triggering default, and that the default probability of the firm is a function of the price process and of the state variable triggering its default.

(a) the default time is an absolutely continuous stopping time with respect to the market filtration and the default intensity is given by the ratio of the conditional default probability to the default-free survival probability, and (b) the default intensity is a martingale in the market’s measure, and hence the default time is a martingalizing stopping time, if and only if the default intensity is constant.

(1) the default time is not necessarily a stopping time, (2) the intensity process is not necessarily adapted to the market’s filtration, (3) the conditional default probabilities are not necessarily increasing functions, and (4) the default spread is a nondecreasing function of the default time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the valuation of credit-sensitive assets, where the default is triggered by a state variable, which cannot be observed by the market.
the valuation of credit-sensitive securities in a model that allows for a general default mechanism and imperfect information.
the valuation of default-sensitive claims when investors cannot observe the default state variable.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have a very good idea how the default process looks like and that we are able to price the default sensitive claims.
the valuation of default-sensitive claims is possible, even in a model with imperfect information, and that the resulting spreads are not necessarily larger than under perfect information.
the model of Daffi and Lando is a special case of the model of Bielecki et al. and that the latter is more general and flexible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the default time in our model is a random variable with a nontrivial distribution, and the intensity process is a random process with a nontrivalent path.

we show that the default time can be characterized by a totally inaccessible random variable, which is not surprising, but that the intensity process is not a predictable process, which is surprising.
we provide a general valuation framework for financial assets subject default risk under imperfect information.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the presence of imperfect information, the default time is not necessarily a stopping time in the filtration generated by the price process, and this feature has important implications in the pricing formulas.
the credit spread is not a function of the intensity process but rather a function of the conditional default probability.
, in the case of default-sensitive claims, the market price of credit risk is not constant but varies with the state variable.
